title: Raw counts don't compare across item sets
statement: When students took different items or forms, never compare or correlate their raw or percent-correct scores; first equate them, or estimate ability from the answers and each item's difficulty.
example: 20 right answers on easy items and 20 on hard ones give the same raw score but different abilities.
detail: A reading assessment's scoring design rejects the sum score because it treats every correct answer alike whatever the item's difficulty, so a student with 20 easy items right and one with 20 hard items right get the same raw score for different abilities (`grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/courses/map-proxy-assessment/validity/01_PSYCHOMETRIC_DESIGN.md`). It estimates each student's ability on the logit scale from the responses and the difficulties of the items that student took, the method the reference test documents (`grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/courses/map-proxy-assessment/validity/MAP_PROXY_VALIDITY_CASE.md`).
against: Under the one-parameter model the package uses, students who took the same items and got the same number right receive the same estimate whichever items those were, so the gain over a raw count lies in comparing different item sets, not in weighting responses within one.

evidence.quote: **Sum score:** Treats every correct answer identically regardless of item difficulty. A student who answered 20 easy items correctly and a student who answered 20 hard items correctly receive the same raw score — which maps to different ability levels. MLEF weights each response by the information content of that item.
A raw sum score treats a correct answer on a b=−2.0 item identically to a correct answer on a b=+1.0 item — MLEF does not.
so the bridge currently supports **neither** a direction nor a magnitude claim
